concerns.text: FR-007 states the system MUST compute [deferred] **prediction intervals** (e.g., via Monte Carlo dropout), while SC-006 later requires coverage of true values within the predicted **90 % confidence intervals**. The use of two different terms for what appears to be the same uncertainty quantification creates unstable terminology.

SC-006 refers to **confidence intervals**, whereas the related functional requirement (FR-007) mentions **prediction intervals**. Consistency of terminology for uncertainty estimates should be enforced.

FR-001 assumes the NASA Ames and University of Wisconsin battery datasets are publicly downloadable, but the project’s research documentation indicates these datasets are not available and a synthetic placeholder will be used. Without real multi‑channel time‑series data the requirement cannot be exercised, making the functional requirement untestable.

SC-004 states the model *aims* for an R² ≥ 0.80 on an unseen‑protocol subset. The word “aims” makes the success criterion non‑deterministic; a test must be able to declare pass/fail. Replace “aims” with a mandatory threshold (e.g., “must achieve”) or add a clear decision rule.

SC-005 requires measuring “percentage of cells successfully processed” but does not define the reference population (original dataset size after filtering, raw download size, etc.). Without a concrete denominator the metric cannot be reproducibly calculated.

SC-009 demands a held‑out test subset with at least 10 cells of unseen cycling protocols. The specification provides no guarantee that the public datasets contain that many distinct protocol types, so the input condition may be unreachable.

SC-003 and SC-008 both require a Spearman ρ ≥ 0.7 between permutation importance and SHAP rankings, resulting in duplicate success criteria. Consolidate to a single criterion to avoid unnecessary redundancy.

FR-001 requires downloading NASA Ames and UW battery datasets with voltage, current, and temperature channels, but the accompanying research.md states that no such open datasets exist and a synthetic placeholder CSV will be used. This makes the core research question (identifying early‑cycle electrochemical signatures) unanswerable with the planned data.

FR-002 mandates resampling to 100 time‑steps per cycle and normalizing using the first 50 cycles, yet the placeholder dataset contains only a single numeric column and lacks the required three‑channel time‑series, violating the functional requirement.

SC-004 expects evaluation on a held‑out test set with unseen cycling protocols (≥10 cells). The placeholder data has no genuine protocol variation, so the protocol‑agnostic validation cannot be performed, breaking the methodological premise of the research question.

The performance budget (≤6 h, ≤7 GB RAM) and 30‑minute hyper‑parameter sweep are calibrated on the synthetic CSV, which does not reflect the size or structure of real battery time‑series data, rendering the power analysis invalid.

FR-007 calls for computing prediction intervals (e.g., via Monte Carlo dropout) against true final capacity fade, but the placeholder dataset provides no genuine capacity‑fade target, making this requirement infeasible.

FR-001 requires downloading NASA Ames and University of Wisconsin battery datasets, yet the accompanying research.md states these datasets are not publicly available and a synthetic placeholder CSV will be used, making the requirement unfulfillable and breaking construct validity.

SC-001 mandates reporting R² against the *actual measured* final capacity fade, but the placeholder dataset lacks genuine capacity‑fade measurements; the target is derived from the same synthetic generation process, so the validation target is not independent of the predictors.

SC-003 requires a Spearman ρ ≥ 0.7 between permutation‑importance ranking and SHAP ranking. Both rankings are computed from the same trained model, so a high correlation is expected by definition, making this a circular validation rather than an independent check.

SC-009 evaluates the predictive power of the top‑5 identified features via a linear regression that must achieve ≥50 % of the full model’s R². Since the top‑5 features are selected based on the model’s own importance scores, this test is tautological and does not provide an independent assessment of feature relevance.

SC-004 aims for R² ≥ 0.80 on a held‑out subset with unseen cycling protocols, yet the placeholder dataset contains no genuine protocol variation, so the claimed generalization test cannot be performed independently of the training data.

FR-007 proposes computing prediction intervals via Monte Carlo dropout on synthetic placeholder data; without real measurement noise the intervals have no meaningful uncertainty interpretation, and SC-006’s coverage claim becomes circular.

SC-006 requires a certain proportion of true final capacity fade values to fall within 90 % confidence intervals, but with synthetic targets the ‘true’ values are defined by the data generation process, rendering the coverage metric non‑independent and circular.

FR-001 requires downloading NASA Ames and University of Wisconsin battery datasets, yet the accompanying research.md states these datasets are not publicly available and a synthetic placeholder CSV will be used, making the requirement unfulfillable and breaking construct validity.

SC-001 mandates reporting R² against the *actual measured* final capacity fade, but the placeholder dataset lacks genuine capacity‑fade measurements; the target is derived from the same synthetic generation process, so the validation target is not independent of the predictors.

SC-003 requires a Spearman ρ ≥ 0.7 between permutation‑importance ranking and SHAP ranking. Both rankings are computed from the same trained model, so a high correlation is expected by definition, making this a circular validation rather than an independent check.

new_concerns.text: SC-001 states that capacity values are generated by a physics‑based simulator, while FR-001 and FR-002 require using real measured capacity fade from the Battery Archive dataset. This creates a contradiction about the source of the target variable.

SC-002 defines success thresholds of ≤4 hours, ≤6 GB RAM, and ≤12 GB disk for computational feasibility, but FR-004 (and FR-007) only require the system to complete within ≤6 hours, ≤7 GB RAM, and ≤14 GB disk. The stricter SC limits conflict with the looser FR limits, leading to an internal inconsistency.

SC-002 lists computational feasibility limits as ≤4 hours, ≤6 GB RAM, ≤12 GB disk, which conflict with the earlier US‑2 description (≤6 hours, ≤7 GB RAM, ≤14 GB disk). The ambiguous thresholds make the success criterion non‑deterministic and untestable. Align the limits to a single, clearly defined set and state the exact measurement procedure.

SC-001 states that R² is measured against “recorded final capacity fade … generated by a physics‑based simulator,” while FR‑001 now requires downloading a real Battery Archive dataset that already contains measured capacity fade. The source of the target values is contradictory, preventing a reproducible evaluation. Clarify whether the target is simulated or measured and ensure the success criterion references the same source as the functional requirement.

SC-008 (Spearman correlation between permutation importance and SHAP rankings) remains a circular validation because both metrics are computed from the same model outputs. This criterion cannot fail unless the model is pathological, thus it does not constitute an empirical test of the claimed insight.

responses.response: Removed all references to NASA Ames / University of Wisconsin datasets. FR-001 and US-1 now name the Battery Archive (batteryarchive.org, DOI 10.24433/CO.0933141.v1) as the sole verified primary source, which is a real, publicly available repository of multi-channel battery cycling data (including NASA and other public cell datasets) with voltage, current, temperature, and capacity measurements. No synthetic placeholder CSV may be used.
